_notes: Aging-curve and dynasty-value parameters. Tune here, never in code.
All ages are player age in the season being valued. Multipliers are
relative to that position's peak (peak = 1.0).
peak: [start, end] ages of the plateau.
rise: per-year multiplier applied for each year BELOW peak start
(a 21yo RB with peak_start 23 plays year 1 at rise^2 of peak).
decline: per-year multiplier for each year past peak end.
cliff: [age, per-year multiplier] — steeper decline from this age.
end: age at which projected value hits zero.
discount: per-year uncertainty discount on future seasons.
market_blend: weight on the dADP-implied value vs the model value.
0 = pure model, 1 = pure market. Rookie committee-backs and
ambiguous roles are why this exists; the model can't see breakouts.
tiers: a break is a gap >= gap_factor * the median gap, floored by
min_gap_pct * the board's total spread (scale-free) and by
min_gap_abs. The floor MUST be relative: an absolute floor was
calibrated for values in the hundreds, and once values became
surplus-over-replacement in the double digits it exceeded the
whole board and put every player in Tier 1.
roster.collision_mult: haircut on a WR/TE who shares a QB with a
pass catcher you already roster — two mouths, one ball. Not a GB
rule; it applies to every team you have a pass catcher on.
roster.handcuff_mult: bump on an RB behind your own RB, applied ONLY
when he has standalone value (surplus over replacement > 0). A
pure insurance back gets no bump; a Stevenson-style goal-line
back does.
roster.scarcity_damp: 0 = pure positional replacement, 1 = one
global bar for every position. Pure positional VORP had a 22-year
old TE worth 3.7x Justin Jefferson, because a one-TE league puts
TE replacement on a much worse player and the multi-year sum then
multiplies that gap ~5x. Scarcity is real, that magnitude is not.
0.35 shrinks cross-position gaps without erasing the effect. Not
fitted — raise it if the board still reads TE-heavy, lower it if
scarce positions stop mattering.
ONE-SIDED: damping only RAISES bars that sit below the global
average. It never lowers one that sits above it. A scarce
position has a low bar because replacement there is a bad
player; a deep position has a high bar because replacement is a
real starter. Two-sided damping cut the 1QB bar ~43 pts/season,
the 20-season discounted sum turned that into ~285 pts of
surplus per quarterback, and the board recommended a QB at every
mid-round pick in a league that starts one. Raising the floor
for scarcity is the goal; subsidising abundance is not.
roster.bench_mult: haircut on a player at a position where you
already fill every dedicated slot AND no flex slot accepts him —
a second QB in a 1QB league, a second DEF. He starts zero games.
Not zero value (injury cover, trade bait) but nothing here can
price that, so 0.25 is a judgement call, unlike the flex-bar
rescale beside it which is exact. Positions that CAN flex are
repriced against the flex bar instead; see saturation_bar().
rise: 8/11 — all four moved to 0.96 from 0.90-0.94. The old values
double-paid for youth. A young player already earns more in this
model by having more seasons in the horizon sum; rise then scaled
every one of those seasons up as well. And the projection being
marked up already embeds expected development — a rookie's 215 is
a forecast that includes his growth, not a suppressed peak. Proof
it was too steep: at rise 0.90 the board preferred Harold Fannin
(22, proj 180, ADP 39) to Ladd McConkey (24, proj 228, ADP 38) —
same round in the market, 48 fewer projected points. At 0.96
McConkey surfaces and so does Trey McBride (26, proj 235). Youth
still wins on horizon alone. Uniform across positions because the
double-count argument is structural, not position-specific; the
direct evidence was at TE and WR.
THESE CURVES ARE PRIORS from consensus aging research, not fitted to
data. Treat every number as arguable and tune against your leagues.

horizons._note: How many seasons you actually hold a player. Full dynasty carries everyone forever, so his whole remaining career counts. A 3-keeper league carries 7 max and churns the rest — you own roughly two more seasons of a veteran before he is traded or let go, so seasons past that should not price him. Using the dynasty horizon in a keeper league over-penalizes age and talks you out of elite older players for younger lesser ones.
